reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Renal agenesis is the complete failure of development of one or both kidneys owing to absent or failed interaction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric blastema; the unilateral form is relatively common and often silent, whereas the bilateral form is rare and incompatible with postnatal life

Bilateral renal agenesis produces the Potter sequence, in which severe oligohydramnios leads to pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures and the characteristic Potter facies, with death usually from respiratory failure
Unilateral renal agenesis is compatible with normal life through compensatory hypertrophy of the solitary kidney and is often found incidentally or on antenatal imaging
Absence of the kidney is typically accompanied by an absent ipsilateral ureter and a hemitrigone, so a missing ureteric orifice is seen at cystoscopy

There is a strong association with genital tract anomalies owing to shared mesonephric and Mullerian development: in girls a unicornuate uterus, Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome or the obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis (OHVIRA / Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich) syndrome, and in boys seminal vesicle cysts or absence of the vas deferens

It may be isolated or part of a syndrome such as the VACTERL association, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, Kallmann syndrome or renal coloboma syndrome, so extrarenal features should prompt genetic evaluation and family screening
Lifelong surveillance of the solitary kidney, with attention to blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function and avoidance of nephrotoxic insults, is advised
reference.pathophysiology: Renal agenesis results from failure of the metanephros to develop, most often because the ureteric bud fails to form from the mesonephric (wolffian) duct, fails to reach the metanephric blastema, or fails to induce it. As the ureteric bud also gives rise to the ureter and the corresponding hemitrigone, its absence explains the missing ipsilateral ureter and hemitrigone. The shared embryological origin with the genital ducts underlies the frequent Mullerian anomalies in females and wolffian anomalies in males. In bilateral agenesis the fetus produces little or no urine; because fetal urine is the principal component of amniotic fluid in the later part of pregnancy, profound oligohydramnios develops, compressing the fetus and preventing normal lung expansion, and so producing the pulmonary hypoplasia and deformational features of the Potter sequence.
additionalDifferentials: Ectopic (for example pelvic) or crossed fused kidney with a kidney present but outside the fossa
A small atrophic kidney from reflux or obstructive nephropathy
An involuted kidney after a vascular insult
Other causes of oligohydramnios such as membrane rupture, uteroplacental insufficiency or bladder outlet obstruction in the bilateral phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal and postnatal renal tract ultrasound to show an empty renal fossa and assess amniotic fluid
DMSA scintigraphy to confirm absence of functioning tissue and exclude an ectopic kidney
MRI, fetal or postnatal, for anatomy and to locate ectopic renal tissue
Pelvic ultrasound or MRI for uterine and genital anomalies in girls, and seminal vesicle assessment in boys
Blood pressure, urinalysis for proteinuria and serum renal function for surveillance of the solitary kidney
Genetic and syndromic evaluation with screening of first-degree relatives where indicated
redFlags: Bilateral agenesis with severe oligohydramnios and anticipated pulmonary hypoplasia requiring perinatal counselling
Hypertension, proteinuria or declining function in a solitary kidney
An acute illness threatening the only functioning kidney
An obstructive genital anomaly such as OHVIRA presenting with cyclical pain around menarche
reference.prognosis: Unilateral renal agenesis with a normal solitary kidney generally has a good prognosis, though it carries a modestly increased lifetime risk of hypertension, proteinuria and chronic kidney disease that warrants monitoring. Bilateral renal agenesis is almost uniformly fatal in the neonatal period from pulmonary hypoplasia, with only rare reported survival following intensive intervention.
pitfalls: Diagnosing agenesis when the kidney is in fact ectopic or crossed and fused, without searching elsewhere
Overlooking associated genital tract anomalies, particularly Mullerian anomalies in girls
Failing to arrange lifelong surveillance of the solitary kidney
Mistaking an involuted multicystic dysplastic kidney for primary agenesis
Not offering genetic counselling and family screening despite recognised heritable forms
